opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to the kind of uncertainty I wanted in my life at that point. At UW, I could see the path pretty clearly: there were great people there, strong groups, and I had a good sense of what the next several years would look like, what problems I'd be working on, and how they would build on what I'd already done. That's a very reasonable choice, and a lot of people do wonderful work that way.

But Stanford felt more open-ended in a way that excited me. The lab environment was in a moment where computer vision, robotics, and machine learning were all colliding, and nobody really knew yet what the right way to bring them together was. That ambiguity was attractive. It felt like I'd have room to define my own problems instead of inheriting a well-scoped one.

The people mattered a lot too. Talking with potential advisors and students there, I got the sense that they cared about big questions, like how a robot could actually learn to do long, complex tasks the way people do, and they were willing to let students take risks chasing those questions, even if the first year or two looked messy.

So it wasn't that one place was better than the other. It was more that I was young, I didn't have much to lose, and I thought: if I'm going to spend five or six years on something, I'd rather bet on the path where I don't fully know the outcome, because that's where I'd probably grow the most. Looking back, that bet shaped a lot of how I think about research today.

r001.rationale: The response says Stanford’s open-ended, ambiguous research environment was exciting because he could define his own problems and did not know the outcome of that path.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a clean, rational decision at the time. At UW I had a really good situation. I knew the people, I knew what the next few years would look like, and I had a line of work in robotics and learning that I could've just kept pushing. That predictability is comforting, especially as a young researcher who's still not totally sure they belong in the field.

But that's also what worried me. I could see the whole path, and it felt like I'd already answered the interesting questions about it. Stanford, when I visited, felt much more chaotic in a good way. People in the vision group, the robotics folks, the NLP people, they were all bumping into each other, and the conversations I had in the hallway were about things I didn't know how to think about yet. Fei-Fei and Silvio's group in particular were asking questions about how perception, interaction, and embodiment fit together, and I didn't have a ready-made opinion. That discomfort was really the attraction.

I also think there's something about being somewhere where you're clearly not the person who knows the most. At UW I was starting to feel like I understood the local landscape, and that's a dangerous place to be as a student, because you stop stretching. At Stanford I was surrounded by people who had taste in problems I hadn't developed yet, and I figured the fastest way to grow was to go absorb that, even if it meant resetting a little.

So the short version is: UW offered me a path I could predict, and Stanford offered me a path where I'd probably be wrong a lot more often. At that stage of my career, being wrong more often seemed like the better bet.

r001.rationale: He says Stanford raised unfamiliar research questions he had no ready opinion about, and that the resulting discomfort and unpredictable path attracted him.

astra-6.text: What excited me was the chance to explore. The path at UW felt more predictable—I could see how the research would develop. Stanford felt more open-ended, with opportunities to encounter different ideas and figure out what I really wanted to work on. That uncertainty was part of the appeal. I wanted to put myself in an environment where I could be surprised and grow.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Stanford was open-ended and offered a chance to encounter different ideas and figure out what he really wanted to work on; it describes that uncertainty as part of the appeal.

sol-6.1.text: What excited me was the chance to explore. At UW, I could see a more predictable path: I knew the environment, and I had a sense of what the next research steps would look like. Stanford felt much more open-ended. There were people approaching robotics and AI from different directions, and I wanted to be somewhere that would challenge my assumptions. That uncertainty was a little scary, but it was also a big part of the appeal.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts knowing the likely next research steps at UW with Stanford’s open-ended path, and says that uncertainty was part of the appeal.
